overview: Two passive transport processes driven by concentration gradients — one general, one specific to water across a semipermeable membrane.
genZNote: Osmosis is just diffusion that only wants water.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: The net movement of any particle (solute or gas) from high to low concentration.
aspects.valueB: The net movement of water specifically, across a semipermeable membrane, from low to high solute concentration.

aspects.label: Substance Moved
aspects.valueA: Any molecule — ions, gases, small solutes.

aspects.label: Membrane Requirement
aspects.valueA: Can occur with or without a membrane (e.g. perfume diffusing through air).
aspects.valueB: Requires a selectively/semipermeable membrane that solutes cannot easily cross.

aspects.label: Driving Force
aspects.valueA: Concentration gradient of the diffusing substance itself.
aspects.valueB: Solute concentration gradient, which indirectly drives water movement toward the more concentrated side.

aspects.label: Biological Example
aspects.valueA: Oxygen diffusing from alveoli into blood.
aspects.valueB: Red blood cells shrinking in a hypertonic solution or swelling/lysing in a hypotonic one.

aspects.label: Limitations / Pitfalls
aspects.valueA: Rate slows as the gradient equalizes; large or charged molecules diffuse very slowly without a channel.
aspects.valueB: Only meaningful when a membrane is at least partly impermeable to the solute; osmotic pressure can be substantial.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: General movement of any substance down its own gradient.
aspects.valueB: Water movement across a membrane driven by a solute gradient.

overlay.memoryTrick: "Osmosis is diffusion's picky cousin — water only, membrane required."
overlay.commonMisconception: Osmosis is not 'water diffusing' in the loose sense — it specifically requires a semipermeable membrane and a solute gradient.
